Hypothesis (final submission text):

"Approximately 45.7% (16/35) of replicated Psychology (rpp) studies were led, in the replication, by a junior-rank author. Specifically, among the 97 Psychology (rpp) studies in the meta-regression dataset, 35 were replicated (replicated == 1, i.e., replication p ≤ 0.05 in the same direction as the original); of these 35, 16 had a most-senior replication author (seniority.r) holding a junior rank — Assistant Professor (10) or Assistant (6). Sensitivity to the junior-rank boundary: if 'junior' means Assistant Professor only, the proportion is 10/35 ≈ 28.6%; if the non-professorial 'Researcher' rank (4 studies) is additionally counted as junior, it rises to 20/35 ≈ 57.1%."

Workflow:
1. Loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows × 57 columns; projects: ml1=592, ml3=220, rpp=97, ee=18).
2. Filtered to project == 'rpp' (Psychology): 97 rows; 35 with replicated == 1 (62 with replicated == 0). No missing values in seniority.r (rpp subset or full file).
3. Tallied seniority.r over the 35 replicated rpp studies: Assistant Professor 10, Professor 8, Associate Professor 7, Assistant 6, Researcher 4.
4. Computed the proportion of studies whose seniority.r is a junior rank (Assistant Professor or Assistant): 16/35 ≈ 45.7%, with the sensitivity variants above.
Assumption noted: the metadata description of seniority.r says "most senior author in the original paper," which is a copy-paste documentation typo (the column sits in the replication .r block, consistent with all other .r columns); seniority.r was treated as the replication-side most senior author, as the question requires. The second CSV was not used — it contains no seniority/author-rank columns.
